articles.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Fends Off ‘Clayface’ for Top Spot on Friday With $3.56 Million
articles.summary: A24’s “You Can See Everything” narrowly beat Warner Bros. and DC’s “Clayface” at the Friday box office, cementing its status as the must-watch documentary — or film, for that matter — of the moment.
body: Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

Just behind the doc, “Clayface” landed at No. 2 on its second Friday, making $3.3 million from 3,478 North American theaters. The gory DC film has made $36.9 million domestically so far, with rival estimates suggesting the film will gross another $10.25 million by Sunday.

articles.title: ‘Ah Girl’ Wins Best Film at Singapore’s Silver Screen Awards as Shahrbanoo Sadat Takes Director Prize
articles.summary: Singaporean filmmaker Ang Geck Geck Priscilla’s debut feature “Ah Girl” won best film in the Asian Feature Film Competition at the Singapore International Film Festival’s Silver Screen Awards on Saturday. The film follows a seven-year-old girl in 1990s Singapore whose parents have separated.
body: Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat won best director for “No Good Men,” which opened the Berlinale. Set in Kabul just before the Taliban come back to power, the drama follows a camerawoman whose work, family and freedom are suddenly in doubt. Sadat, who has lived in Germany since 2021, made the 2016 Cannes premiere “Wolf and Sheep” and 2019’s “The Orphanage.”

The jury split the best performance prize. Pushpa Thing Lama was honored for “Elephants in the Fog,” about a member of Nepal’s third-gender Kinnar community searching for her missing daughter. Putri Marino shared the award for “Four Seasons in Java,” a magical realist drama about a woman who goes back to her hometown after two decades behind bars.

The Special Jury Prize went to Japanese director Nagahisa Makoto’s “Burn,” his second feature, which premiered at Sundance. Nagahisa won awards at the same festival for his short “And So We Put Goldfish in the Pool” (2017) and his feature “We Are Little Zombies” (2019).

articles.title: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry
articles.summary: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more. Man’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend…
body: “A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”

A 2024 study of US Google searches noted an increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.

articles.title: Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59
articles.summary: Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta, whose credits include the crime thriller “Kaante,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-starring “Kaabil,” has died following a fall at his Mumbai residence on Oct. 30. He was 59, according to the Press Trust of India.
body: Police in Mumbai’s Versova neighborhood have filed an accidental death report. Deputy Commissioner of Police Purushottam Karad told the Free Press Journal that members of Gupta’s family were sleeping when the incident occurred and became aware of it the following morning. “The family has not raised any suspicion or lodged a complaint,” Karad said.

Gupta was a prominent exponent of the glossy, action-driven Hindi-language crime thriller, bringing a visual sensibility heavily indebted to Hollywood to an industry traditionally dominated by melodrama and musicals. His career behind the camera began with “Aatish: Feel the Fire” in 1994, featuring Sanjay Dutt and Aditya Pancholi. He subsequently directed “Ram Shastra,” “Jung” and “Khauff,” developing an enduring professional relationship with Dutt that extended across 10 films, including projects Gupta produced.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
articles.summary: The second series of the hit show reached its climax on Friday after attracting 15 million viewers.
body: We've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.
The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.
They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.
The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.

articles.title: Black Doves actress says she loved playing 'a very Welsh assassin'
articles.summary: Gabrielle Creevy says she auditioned for the role using her Welsh accent "and they loved it".
body: Award-winning actress Gabrielle Creevy has told how she loved being able to play "a very Welsh assassin" in the upcoming new season of spy thriller Black Doves.
Creevy plays the role of Eleanor in the Netflix drama, starring alongside actors including Keira Knightley, Sarah Lancashire and Ben Whishaw.
The Port Talbot-born actress told Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales she had auditioned with a Welsh accent "and they kind of loved it", with the show writing in extra details to add to her character.
"I'm kind of thrilled that they went with it because as a kid growing up and watching things, there was never that, there was never the Welsh accent," she said.

articles.title: Aaron Paul's Clayface Deleted Scenes Explained By Director James Watkins
articles.summary: Aaron Paul has a strange, quick cameo in Clayface,, and now the film's director James Watkins is confirming the existence of Paul's deleted scenes.
body: "Clayface" has one of the most confusing cameos in any major studio release this year. In the movie's third act action sequence, Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) storms a nightclub filled with the gangsters who attacked him and scarred his face. During the scene, he briefly takes on the appearance of a man played by actor Aaron Paul (best known as Jesse Pinkman on "Breaking Bad").

"At one point, we were looking at [Matt's character arc] and thinking, Is it the 'sins of the father'? But actually, as we worked on the script, I thought that notion of revenge was more universal and more relatable to all of us. It doesn't matter whether you're carrying a trauma or any of that. If we're slighted, we carry this sense of being wronged and we all want to do something, but generally in life we can't do anything about it and we're powerless."

"Clayface" loosely adapts the "Batman: The Animated Series" episode "Feat of Clay." That episode certainly needed no childhood backstory for Matt Hagen (Ron Perlman) – he was just an actor hit with bad luck desperate to save his career and the fame it granted him.

articles.title: Brit School North arts college plan given go-ahead
articles.summary: Inspired by the world-famous Brit School, the college will be built in the centre of Bradford.
body: Plans for the north of England's first Brit School-inspired performing arts college have been approved.
Inspired by the world-famous arts academy in London which produced talents such as Adele and Tom Holland, Brit North is expected to bring more than 550 students and staff into the city centre.
The college will be housed on the site of the former Jacob's Well council building, which is currently a car park, and aims to open by 2028.
The project, which has been approved by Bradford Council, is spearheaded by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) who are owners and organisers of the music showcase, the Brit Awards.

articles.title: 5 Best Movies Like Love Of Your Life
articles.summary: Love of Your Life, starring Margaret Qualley, isn't about romance so much as grief and loss, much like these other movies worth checking out.
body: Margaret Qualley's "Love of Your Life" has become a big hit on Prime Video. The Rachel Morrison-directed drama stars Qualley as Maya, a Boston nurse whose husband passes away during the global pandemic of 2020. Those expecting a romance along the lines of the film's fellow Prime Video hit "The Map that Leads to You," however, may have been surprised to learn that this movie isn't actually as interested in the "love" part of its title as it may have appeared at first glance, as it instead delivers a candid exploration of grief.

The film sees Maya retreat from society following her husband's passing. Clearly suppressing her feelings, she refuses to acknowledge her loss, literally running away from Boston and living a clandestine life in various countries around the world. It's not until she reunites with an old friend and decides to return to the home of her former mother-in-law, Catherine Keener's Ruth, that she finally accepts her loss and learns to value the life she still has. As Ruth tells her, "Stay in love with your own life while it's happening."
